meta.name: Drug classes
meta.about: Drug classes: how a family of medicines works, what it targets in the body, which conditions it treats and which medications on this site belong to it. Educational, not prescribing advice.

calcium-channel-blockers.name: Calcium channel blockers
calcium-channel-blockers.summary: Medicines that relax the muscle in artery walls (and, for some members, slow the heart) by blocking the calcium channels those muscles need to contract. Used mainly for high blood pressure and angina.
calcium-channel-blockers.mechanism: Muscle cells contract when calcium enters through L-type channels in their membrane. Blocking the channel leaves arterial smooth muscle relaxed, so arteries widen, resistance falls and blood pressure drops; coronary arteries widen too, improving supply in angina. The dihydropyridines (amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine) act almost only on vessels. Verapamil and diltiazem also block the channels in the heart's conduction tissue and muscle, slowing the rate and reducing force, which makes them useful for fast rhythms but hazardous with beta blockers or in heart failure.

ace-inhibitors.name: ACE inhibitors
ace-inhibitors.summary: Medicines ending in -pril that block the enzyme which makes angiotensin II, lowering blood pressure, unloading a failing heart and protecting the kidneys in diabetes.
ace-inhibitors.mechanism: The kidneys release renin when pressure or salt falls; renin makes angiotensin I, and angiotensin-converting enzyme in the lungs and vessels turns it into angiotensin II, which constricts arteries, releases aldosterone (salt and water retention) and thickens heart muscle. Blocking the enzyme removes all of these effects, and the pressure inside the kidney's filters falls, which slows the leak of protein in diabetic kidney disease. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so it accumulates and causes the characteristic dry cough.

angiotensin-receptor-blockers.name: Angiotensin receptor blockers
angiotensin-receptor-blockers.summary: Medicines ending in -sartan that block the receptor angiotensin II acts on. They do the same job as ACE inhibitors without the cough, and are the usual alternative when an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated.
angiotensin-receptor-blockers.mechanism: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by binding AT1 receptors on arterial muscle, the adrenal cortex and heart muscle. ARBs occupy those receptors so the hormone cannot act: arteries relax, aldosterone falls and the heart and kidneys are spared its growth-promoting effects. Because ACE is untouched, bradykinin is not raised and cough and angio-oedema are rare.

beta-blockers.name: Beta blockers
beta-blockers.summary: Medicines ending in -olol that shield the heart from adrenaline, slowing it and reducing its oxygen demand. Core treatment for angina, after heart attacks, in heart failure and for controlling fast rhythms. Selective (cardioselective) agents such as bisoprolol, atenolol and metoprolol are used mainly for heart problems, while non-selective ones such as propranolol also treat the physical symptoms of anxiety, tremor, migraine and an overactive thyroid, and eye-drop forms lower pressure in glaucoma. For high blood pressure on its own they are now reserved for people in whom other medicines have not worked. They are prescription-only, tiredness is their commonest drawback, and once started they are reduced gradually rather than stopped abruptly.
beta-blockers.mechanism: Adrenaline and noradrenaline speed and strengthen the heart through beta-1 receptors. Beta blockers occupy the receptors so the heart beats more slowly and less forcefully, uses less oxygen and lets fewer atrial impulses through the AV node. Cardioselective members (bisoprolol, metoprolol, atenolol) mostly spare the beta-2 receptors in the airways; non-selective ones (propranolol) block both and can provoke asthma. In heart failure, protecting the heart from chronic adrenaline drive improves survival when started low and increased slowly. Blocking beta-1 receptors lowers contractility, heart rate and the speed of conduction through the nodes; metoprolol, for example, flattens the slow depolarisation of pacemaker cells so they fire less often. Blood pressure falls through several routes, including less renin release from the kidney. Propranolol has additional membrane-stabilising properties that contribute to its antiarrhythmic effect, and because it is non-selective it also blunts the tremor, palpitations and sweating driven by adrenaline in anxiety and thyrotoxicosis. Beyond the heart the class is used for essential tremor, portal hypertension, aortic dissection, long QT syndrome and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; short-acting intravenous agents such as esmolol are used in intensive care for fast rhythms, and labetalol mainly for hypertensive emergencies. The same receptor blockade explains the drawbacks: beta-2 blockade can tighten airways and peripheral vessels, and by damping the adrenaline response the drugs can hide the shaking and racing heart that warn of hypoglycaemia in people with diabetes.

statins.name: Statins
statins.summary: The main cholesterol-lowering medicines. They cut LDL cholesterol by 30-55% and reduce heart attacks and strokes in anyone at raised cardiovascular risk.
statins.mechanism: Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that controls how much cholesterol the liver makes. The liver compensates by displaying more LDL receptors, pulling LDL out of the blood. Lower LDL means less cholesterol deposited in artery walls, and statins also stabilise existing plaques so they are less likely to rupture and cause a clot. High-intensity statins (atorvastatin 40-80 mg, rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) are used after heart attacks and strokes.

loop-diuretics.name: Loop diuretics
loop-diuretics.summary: Powerful diuretics that make the kidneys excrete salt and water within an hour. Used to clear fluid in heart failure, kidney and liver disease. Furosemide, bumetanide and torasemide are the 'high-ceiling' diuretics whose effect keeps growing with the dose, so they are chosen when fluid must be shifted quickly or in large amounts. Their power is also their hazard: the same salt and water loss can cause dehydration, low blood pressure and disturbed potassium, sodium and magnesium, so kidney function and electrolytes are checked after starting and the medicine may be paused during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever.
loop-diuretics.mechanism: They block the sodium-potassium-chloride co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, the segment that normally reabsorbs a quarter of filtered sodium. Furosemide competes with chloride for its binding site on the transporter, and because less salt is reabsorbed the medullary interstitium becomes less concentrated, so the kidney also loses much of its ability to reclaim free water. Salt that stays in the tubule carries water with it, so urine output rises several-fold. Potassium, magnesium and calcium are lost through the same blockade, and the resulting hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, metabolic alkalosis and raised uric acid are the predictable laboratory consequences, with hyponatraemia and dehydration when intake does not keep pace. Loop diuretics also reach the inner ear, where they alter the fluid of the stria vascularis and lower the electrical potential the cochlea depends on; the hearing loss this causes is usually temporary, but it can be permanent in severe kidney failure or when combined with other ototoxic drugs such as aminoglycoside antibiotics, whose blood levels furosemide can also raise. Thiazide-like diuretics (indapamide, bendroflumethiazide) act further along the nephron and are the gentler class used for blood pressure.

anticoagulants.name: Anticoagulants
anticoagulants.summary: Medicines that slow the clotting cascade to prevent and treat clots in veins and the heart: strokes in atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. The class spans the direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran), the vitamin K antagonist warfarin and the injectable heparins. UK guidance now favours a direct oral anticoagulant for most people with atrial fibrillation who need stroke prevention, keeping warfarin for those in whom the newer drugs are contraindicated, not tolerated or unsuitable; warfarin also remains the recommended choice for mechanical heart valves. Every member trades a lower risk of harmful clots for a higher risk of bleeding, so the decision to start, to pause for a procedure or to stop is always a balance made with the prescriber.
anticoagulants.mechanism: Direct oral anticoagulants block a single clotting enzyme: factor Xa (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or thrombin (dabigatran), with a predictable effect that needs no blood-level monitoring. Warfarin instead starves the liver of usable vitamin K, so factors II, VII, IX and X are made in inactive form; its effect builds over days and varies with diet and other drugs, so the INR test tunes the dose. Heparins, given by injection, activate antithrombin and are used in hospital and pregnancy. Unfractionated heparin is a mixture of sulphated sugar chains whose negative charges bind antithrombin and change its shape, turning it from a slow inhibitor of thrombin and factor Xa into a very fast one; the shorter low-molecular-weight heparins (enoxaparin, dalteparin) carry the key pentasaccharide sequence and act mainly on factor Xa. Warfarin's block of vitamin K epoxide reductase also affects the natural anticoagulants protein C and protein S, and because warfarin is cleared through several cytochrome P450 enzymes its effect shifts with many other medicines. The factor Xa inhibitors act on Xa within the prothrombinase complex, so prothrombin is no longer converted to thrombin; dabigatran binds thrombin itself. The laboratory reflects these differences: heparin is followed with the aPTT or an anti-Xa level, warfarin with the prothrombin time expressed as the INR, while DOACs are given at fixed doses without routine blood-level checks. Reversal is likewise drug-specific: vitamin K for warfarin, protamine for heparin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, and andexanet alfa, which NICE recommends for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding on apixaban or rivaroxaban.

antiplatelets.name: Antiplatelet drugs
antiplatelets.summary: Medicines that stop platelets clumping into the clots that block arteries. The backbone of treatment after heart attacks, strokes and stents.
antiplatelets.mechanism: Platelets plug damaged vessels by sticking to each other; in a diseased artery the plug becomes the clot that causes a heart attack or stroke. Low-dose aspirin permanently disables COX-1 in platelets so they cannot make thromboxane; clopidogrel, ticagrelor and prasugrel block the P2Y12 receptor that responds to ADP. After a stent both are used together for months, because a clot on the stent is a catastrophe.

nitrates.name: Nitrates
nitrates.summary: Vasodilators that relieve angina within minutes by relaxing veins and coronary arteries. Available as a spray for attacks and as long-acting tablets for prevention. Glyceryl trinitrate under the tongue works within a few minutes and is used both to treat an attack and before exertion that is known to bring one on; isosorbide mononitrate and dinitrate are the longer-acting tablets for prevention, and intravenous infusions are used in hospital. Nitrates relieve the symptom rather than the underlying coronary disease, and their chief practical limits are headache, a fall in blood pressure and the tolerance that develops with round-the-clock exposure.
nitrates.mechanism: Nitrates release nitric oxide inside vascular smooth muscle, which raises cyclic GMP and relaxes the vessel. Veins dilate most, so less blood returns to the heart and its workload and oxygen demand fall; coronary arteries and collaterals widen, improving supply to ischaemic muscle. Continuous exposure causes tolerance, so long-acting preparations are timed to leave a nitrate-free interval each day. Nitrates are converted in the body to nitric oxide, which activates guanylyl cyclase to turn GTP into cyclic GMP; the pooling of blood in dilated veins is the main therapeutic effect, since it lowers the volume returning to the heart (preload) and so the work the ventricle must do. Taken under the tongue the drug acts within minutes, which suits an attack; swallowed long-acting forms are built for steady prevention. Tolerance develops within about a day of continuous exposure and the clinical effect fades, so long-acting regimens leave a daily nitrate-free or low-nitrate period, and continuous intravenous infusions in hospital face the same problem; proposed explanations include oxidative stress in the vessel wall and increased breakdown of cyclic GMP. The interaction with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil) follows directly from the chemistry: these drugs stop cyclic GMP being broken down, so the two together cause a profound fall in blood pressure and fainting, and the combination is absolutely contraindicated.

nsaids.name: NSAIDs
nsaids.summary: Painkillers that also reduce inflammation and fever: ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac and the COX-2 selective coxibs. Excellent for short-term musculoskeletal pain, hazardous when used long term without care. Heartburn, indigestion, stomach pain and feeling or being sick are the common effects; ulcers and bleeding can occur without warning and may be fatal, and NSAIDs account for a large share of all reported adverse drug reactions. Clinicians therefore use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, give oral forms with or just after food, never combine two NSAIDs (including over-the-counter products) and avoid the class altogether in late pregnancy, in people with previous NSAID-related asthma, hives or anaphylaxis, and around heart bypass surgery. Topical gels deliver far lower systemic exposure and are preferred for localised joint and soft-tissue pain.
nsaids.mechanism: NSAIDs block the cyclo-oxygenase enzymes COX-1 and COX-2, cutting production of prostaglandins, the local messengers that sensitise pain nerves, dilate vessels in inflamed tissue and reset the brain's thermostat in fever. The same prostaglandins protect the stomach lining and keep blood flowing through the kidney, so ulcers, kidney injury, fluid retention and raised blood pressure are the class hazards. COX-2 selective agents spare the stomach somewhat but carry more cardiovascular risk. The two isoforms behave differently. COX-1 is present all the time and supports the stomach lining, kidney function and platelet aggregation, so gastric irritation and bleeding are largely COX-1 effects; COX-2 is mostly induced at sites of inflammation and is the main source of the prostaglandins that drive pain, swelling and fever. Most NSAIDs inhibit both isoforms; aspirin inhibits COX-1 more than COX-2, while celecoxib is COX-2 selective. In the kidney, prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, so blocking them reduces glomerular filtration, blunts the natriuresis produced by diuretics and weakens the benefit of ACE inhibitors; the same sodium retention raises blood pressure. The cardiovascular hazard is explained by suppression of COX-dependent prostacyclin, the vessel wall's natural antithrombotic signal, and the thrombotic risk of a given drug depends on how selective it is for COX-2 over COX-1. Hypersensitivity reactions, from an asthma attack or urticaria to anaphylaxis, are linked to COX-1 inhibition with IgE- and T-cell-mediated components, and a person who has reacted to one NSAID is assumed to react to the others.

non-opioid-analgesics.name: Non-opioid analgesics
non-opioid-analgesics.summary: First-line painkillers without opioid or anti-inflammatory action: paracetamol (acetaminophen) above all, safe at normal doses for most people and most types of mild to moderate pain. NHS information describes paracetamol as a common painkiller and fever reducer that very rarely causes side effects when taken correctly; it can take up to an hour to work and keeps working for about five hours, and regular use over many years is regarded as safe provided the recommended dose is never exceeded. Unlike the NSAIDs it has no peripheral anti-inflammatory action and causes far fewer stomach problems, which is why it sits at the first step of most pain ladders and is combined with, rather than replaced by, other painkillers when pain is more severe.
non-opioid-analgesics.mechanism: Paracetamol acts mainly in the central nervous system, weakly inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase in the brain and spinal cord and, through its metabolite AM404, engaging cannabinoid and TRPV1 pathways that raise the pain threshold and lower the fever set-point. It has almost no effect on inflammation or the stomach lining. Its danger is the liver: in overdose a toxic metabolite overwhelms the liver's glutathione and destroys hepatocytes. The exact mechanism is still debated. StatPearls notes that paracetamol is historically grouped with the NSAIDs because it inhibits the cyclo-oxygenase pathway, yet it appears to do so in the central nervous system rather than in peripheral tissues, so reduced prostaglandin synthesis in the brain and spinal cord accounts for the analgesic and antipyretic effect without the anti-inflammatory, gastric and platelet effects of the NSAIDs. Most of a dose is handled by the liver through phase II glucuronidation and sulphation; only a small fraction passes through cytochrome P450 enzymes, chiefly CYP2E1, forming the reactive intermediate NAPQI. At therapeutic doses NAPQI is swiftly conjugated with hepatic glutathione into harmless cysteine and mercaptate compounds that leave in the urine. In overdose the conjugation pathways are saturated, more drug is diverted through CYP450, the limited glutathione stores are exhausted and NAPQI binds covalently to cysteine groups on liver proteins, particularly mitochondrial proteins, causing oxidative injury, failure of mitochondrial ATP synthesis and necrosis of the centrilobular (zone 3) hepatocytes. N-acetylcysteine, which restores glutathione, is the only approved antidote and is close to fully protective when started early after ingestion, which is why hospitals treat on the basis of the dose and timing rather than waiting for symptoms.

opioids.name: Opioids
opioids.summary: Strong painkillers that act on the body's own endorphin receptors: morphine, codeine, tramadol, oxycodone, fentanyl. Essential for severe acute pain and cancer pain; harmful when used long term for chronic non-cancer pain.
opioids.mechanism: Opioids bind mu-opioid receptors in the spinal cord, brainstem and brain, closing the gate on pain signals entering the cord and dampening the emotional response to pain. The same receptors in the brainstem slow breathing, in the gut cause constipation, and in the reward pathways produce euphoria and, with repeated use, tolerance and dependence. Naloxone displaces opioids from the receptors and reverses overdose within minutes.

biguanides.name: Biguanides
biguanides.summary: Metformin is the only biguanide in routine use and the first-line tablet for type 2 diabetes: it lowers glucose without causing hypoglycaemia or weight gain.
biguanides.mechanism: Metformin reduces the glucose the liver pours into the blood by dampening gluconeogenesis, makes muscle and fat more sensitive to insulin so they take up more glucose, and slightly reduces glucose absorption from the gut. It does not stimulate insulin release, which is why it does not cause low blood sugar on its own. HbA1c falls by about 11 mmol/mol (1%).

insulins.name: Insulins
insulins.summary: Injected replacements for the hormone the pancreas no longer makes or cannot make enough of: essential in type 1 diabetes and used in type 2 diabetes when tablets are not enough. Regimens are built from insulins of different speeds: rapid-acting analogues taken with meals, intermediate and long-acting insulins taken once or twice daily as background, and ready-mixed (biphasic) insulins taken before meals; a once-weekly basal insulin (icodec) now also exists. Insulin is given by pen, syringe or pump into the fat under the skin, and the dose is adjusted continually against glucose readings, food, activity and illness. Hypoglycaemia is the price of effective treatment, so recognising and treating a 'hypo' is part of every insulin user's education.
insulins.mechanism: Insulin binds receptors on muscle, fat and liver cells, moving glucose transporters to the cell surface so glucose leaves the blood, switching the liver from making glucose to storing glycogen, and stopping fat breakdown and ketone production. Modern analogues are engineered to act fast at meals (aspart, lispro, glulisine) or flat over 24 hours or more as background (glargine, detemir, degludec); mixed and pump regimens mimic the natural pattern of a basal trickle with mealtime bursts. Rapid-acting analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) are absorbed quickly after injection and lower glucose mainly by increasing uptake into skeletal muscle and fat. Glargine takes the opposite approach: it is soluble in the acidic solution of the pen but precipitates at the neutral pH of tissue, forming a depot that releases insulin slowly over about a day; detemir and degludec achieve a similarly flat profile by other means. In type 1 diabetes the usual pattern is a basal insulin once or twice daily plus a rapid-acting insulin before meals, the basal dose controlling the glucose the liver releases between meals and overnight; in type 2 diabetes treatment may start with a basal insulin alone, add mealtime doses later, or use a mixed insulin before meals. Insulin is injected into the abdomen, outer thighs or buttocks with a fresh needle each time, moving each injection at least a centimetre from the last, because repeated injection into one spot causes fatty lumps (lipohypertrophy) from which absorption is unreliable.

thyroid-hormones.name: Thyroid hormones
thyroid-hormones.summary: Synthetic thyroxine (levothyroxine) replaces what an underactive thyroid cannot make, restoring metabolic rate; the dose is tuned by the TSH blood test. Because the tablet replaces a hormone the body lacks rather than adding a foreign drug, it rarely causes side effects at the right dose: the symptoms that do appear (insomnia, headache, anxiety, sweating, hair loss, loose stools, shaky hands) are the signs of too much, and many years of over-replacement can contribute to osteoporosis and heart trouble. Treatment is usually lifelong; doctors start low, adjust the dose on blood tests, and warn that some people feel better within weeks while others take months. Most adults and children can take it, it is continued through pregnancy with closer blood-test monitoring, and it is usually compatible with breastfeeding.
thyroid-hormones.mechanism: Levothyroxine is identical to the thyroid's own T4. Tissues convert it to active T3, which enters cell nuclei and switches on genes controlling metabolic rate, heat production, heart rate, gut motility, growth and brain development. As levels normalise, the pituitary's TSH falls back into range, which is how the dose is checked. Liothyronine (T3) is used rarely, on specialist advice. The thyroid itself releases mostly T4 and only a minority of the body's T3; the rest is made in the tissues by deiodinase enzymes, especially type 2, and in someone whose thyroid has been removed these enzymes are the only source of T3. Roughly half of a levothyroxine dose is converted this way. T3 enters the nucleus and alters the transcription of genes that set the pace of metabolism, which is why the effect on symptoms lags weeks behind a dose change. The TSH test is the preferred monitor because the pituitary is so sensitive to small shifts in free T4 that TSH moves out of range before free T4 does; a normal TSH is taken as evidence the dose is right. A small group of people have persistent symptoms despite a normal TSH, and a normal TSH does not guarantee a normal T3 in every patient, perhaps because peripheral conversion is impaired; this is the rationale for the specialist-only use of liothyronine (synthetic T3), which in the NHS is started by endocrinologists under shared-care arrangements. Absorption from the gut is incomplete and is reduced by food, coffee, calcium and iron, so the tablet is taken on an empty stomach at the same time each day, and the dose is reviewed when any interacting medicine starts or stops.

bronchodilators.name: Bronchodilators
bronchodilators.summary: Inhaled medicines that relax the muscle around the airways within minutes (salbutamol, terbutaline) or for 12-24 hours (salmeterol, formoterol, and the antimuscarinics tiotropium and ipratropium). They relieve wheeze but do not treat the inflammation behind asthma.
bronchodilators.mechanism: Beta-2 agonists stimulate beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, raising cyclic AMP so the muscle relaxes and the airway widens. Antimuscarinic bronchodilators block the vagal acetylcholine signal that tightens airways and drives mucus, and are especially useful in COPD. Long-acting beta agonists must be paired with an inhaled steroid in asthma, because used alone they mask worsening inflammation and have been linked to asthma deaths.

corticosteroids.name: Corticosteroids
corticosteroids.summary: Synthetic versions of cortisol that switch off inflammation of any cause: inhaled for asthma, as tablets or injections for flares of many diseases, and as creams, drops and joint injections for local use. Short courses are generally well tolerated, but with high doses, long courses or several steroid products used together the hazards mount: bone loss, raised blood sugar, infection, eye and mood changes, and suppression of the body's own cortisol. In the UK, people on longer or higher-dose treatment carry a blue steroid card, and those judged at risk of adrenal insufficiency carry a red emergency card, so that any clinician treating them knows to continue the medicine and cover illness or surgery rather than let the dose lapse.
corticosteroids.mechanism: Glucocorticoids enter cells and bind receptors that move to the nucleus, where they switch off genes for inflammatory cytokines and switch on anti-inflammatory ones, shrinking the whole inflammatory response regardless of its trigger. The same receptors in liver, bone, skin, eye and brain produce the side effects of systemic use, and prolonged dosing suppresses the pituitary-adrenal axis, so the body stops making its own cortisol. Inhaled and topical forms deliver tiny doses where they are needed and largely avoid these effects. Alongside this slow genomic route, a faster non-genomic effect appears within minutes of a dose, including inhibition of phospholipase A2, which starves the inflammatory cascade of arachidonic acid. The synthetic agents (prednisolone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone, betamethasone) tend to produce more Cushingoid change and more suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis than hydrocortisone; dose and duration are surprisingly poor predictors of who will be suppressed, and even inhaled and topical preparations can do it. Suppression may persist for up to a year after stopping, which is why doses are tapered and why hydrocortisone, whose short action lets the axis recover between doses, is the replacement used if adrenal insufficiency develops. Recovery of the axis is assessed with a morning cortisol and, where needed, a short Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test. The symptoms of steroid-induced adrenal insufficiency are non-specific and overlap with both the disease being treated and the withdrawal syndrome itself, so clinicians keep a low threshold for suspecting it.

proton-pump-inhibitors.name: Proton pump inhibitors
proton-pump-inhibitors.summary: The strongest acid-reducing medicines (omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole), which heal ulcers and reflux by shutting down the acid pumps in the stomach lining. They are used for heartburn and acid reflux, indigestion, stomach and duodenal ulcers, and alongside antibiotics to clear Helicobacter pylori. Relief begins within a few days but full effect can take weeks. Most adults can take them, and children can when prescribed; low-dose products are sold over the counter for short courses in adults, with persisting symptoms a reason to see a doctor. Because the serious risks (low magnesium, weakened bones and fractures, gut infections, vitamin B12 deficiency) rise with duration, long-term use is reviewed regularly and stopped or stepped down when it is no longer needed.
proton-pump-inhibitors.mechanism: PPIs irreversibly block the hydrogen-potassium ATPase, the proton pump in parietal cells that secretes acid as the final common step of every stimulus. Acid output falls by over 90% and recovers only as new pumps are made, so the effect outlasts the drug. Taken 30-60 minutes before breakfast when the pumps are most active. H2 blockers (famotidine) are the milder alternative. PPIs are prodrugs: absorbed in the proximal small bowel and carried in the blood to the parietal cells, they are activated only by acid-catalysed cleavage inside the acidic secretory canaliculi, which is why they act so selectively on the pump that makes acid. They are metabolised in the liver mainly by CYP2C19, the route behind their interactions and the variation in exposure between individuals. Suppressing acid has consequences beyond the ulcer: stomach acid normally kills swallowed microbes, so profound suppression allows microbial overgrowth and a higher susceptibility to gut and respiratory infections, including Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea. Absorption of some nutrients also depends on acid, which accounts for the vitamin B12 and iron deficiency seen with long use; hypomagnesaemia is rare, is most likely in people also taking a diuretic, and appears to reflect reduced intestinal absorption rather than renal loss. Acute interstitial nephritis is a recognised but uncommon reaction. Many of the other long-term associations reported, such as kidney, liver and cardiovascular disease and dementia, rest on observational data of low grade, so the practical response is the smallest effective dose for the shortest time rather than avoidance of a very effective class.

penicillins.name: Penicillins
penicillins.summary: The oldest family of antibiotics and still the first choice for many chest, ear, throat, skin and dental infections: amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin and benzylpenicillin.
penicillins.mechanism: Penicillins bind the enzymes bacteria use to cross-link the peptidoglycan of their cell wall; growing bacteria with a weakened wall burst. Human cells have no cell wall, which makes the class remarkably selective. Bacteria resist by making beta-lactamase enzymes that destroy the drug; clavulanic acid in co-amoxiclav blocks the enzyme, and flucloxacillin is built to withstand the staphylococcal version. They are useless against viruses.

antihistamines.name: Antihistamines
antihistamines.summary: Medicines that block histamine's H1 receptors to relieve hay fever, hives and itching. Newer members (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) cause little drowsiness; older ones (chlorphenamine, promethazine) sedate. Second-generation agents are recommended first for allergic rhinitis and urticaria because they work as well with far fewer effects on the brain; fexofenadine is the least likely of all to cause drowsiness. The sedating first-generation drugs (chlorphenamine, promethazine, hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine) still have a place when itching or a streaming nose stops sleep, and some are used for nausea and travel sickness, but their anticholinergic actions make them a poor choice for older people.
antihistamines.mechanism: When mast cells release histamine in an allergic reaction, it makes capillaries leak (swelling, runny nose), stimulates itch nerves and constricts airways. Antihistamines occupy the H1 receptors so these effects are muted. Second-generation drugs cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, which is why they are much less sedating. They are adjuncts only in anaphylaxis, where adrenaline is the treatment. The difference between the generations is largely physical chemistry: the first-generation drugs are lipophilic enough to enter the brain, where blocking H1 receptors produces sedation and slows psychomotor function, and they also block muscarinic receptors, causing dry mouth, blurred vision and difficulty passing urine. Second-generation drugs act mainly on peripheral H1 receptors and penetrate the brain poorly, so they relieve sneezing, itch, hives and watery eyes with little sleepiness, although drowsiness can still appear, particularly at higher-than-usual doses. Because of this profile, current guidelines favour second-generation agents as first-line treatment for allergic rhinitis and urticaria, and they are also preferred when an antihistamine is needed during breastfeeding. Alcohol, sleeping tablets and some antidepressants add to the sedation of the older drugs, and in older adults the first-generation agents are linked to confusion, falls and fractures.

ssris.name: SSRIs
ssris.summary: The most widely used antidepressants (sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine), also first-line for anxiety disorders, panic, OCD and PTSD. The NHS describes them as the usual first choice when an antidepressant is needed, mainly for depression that is persistent or severe, and usually alongside a talking therapy such as cognitive behavioural therapy rather than instead of it. Early side effects (nausea, agitation, sleep change) are common but mostly settle over the first weeks, while sexual problems can persist for as long as the medicine is taken. The medicines are not addictive in the sense of craving or tolerance, but stopping suddenly produces a discontinuation syndrome, so courses are ended by gradual reduction.
ssris.mechanism: SSRIs block the transporter that pumps serotonin back into nerve endings after release, so more remains in the synapse. The clinical benefit arrives over weeks as receptors adapt and neuroplasticity in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex increases; the immediate rise in serotonin mostly produces the early side effects. They are generally safe in overdose and after heart attacks (sertraline). Serotonin released into the synapse is normally pulled back into the nerve ending by the serotonin transporter; SSRIs occupy that transporter, so each burst of serotonin lingers and acts for longer. Too much serotonin signalling produces serotonin syndrome, which StatPearls describes as a triad of altered mental state, autonomic overactivity and neuromuscular signs: agitation, fast heart rate, high blood pressure, fever, brisk reflexes, tremor, nausea, vomiting and clonus; it almost always follows combining an SSRI with another serotonergic medicine or St John's wort, and treatment is to stop the offending drugs with supportive care and benzodiazepines for agitation. Other class effects have their own mechanisms. Serotonin is needed for platelets to aggregate, which explains easy bruising and the bleeding risk, especially with NSAIDs, aspirin and anticoagulants. Citalopram blocks a cardiac potassium channel and so prolongs the QT interval in a dose-dependent way, with the risk of torsades de pointes. Hyponatraemia arises mostly in older people, and the risk is higher with other sodium-lowering drugs, low body weight, female sex, a low baseline sodium and severe illness. Discontinuation symptoms (dizziness, lethargy, sleep disturbance, sensory and gut symptoms, then low mood or anxiety within days) are thought to reflect a sudden fall in synaptic serotonin while receptors remain down-regulated; they are more frequent with short-half-life drugs such as paroxetine and least with fluoxetine, whose long half-life gives a built-in taper.

xanthine-oxidase-inhibitors.name: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors
xanthine-oxidase-inhibitors.summary: Medicines that lower uric acid by blocking the enzyme that makes it, dissolving the crystals that cause gout attacks and tophi when taken every day. Allopurinol is the first choice; it is also used to prevent uric acid kidney stones and to protect the kidneys from the surge of uric acid released when some cancer treatments destroy large numbers of cells. It takes several weeks to bring uric acid down, and the dose is built up gradually because starting high, or stopping for a few days and restarting at the old dose, raises the risk of a severe skin reaction. Febuxostat is the alternative for people who cannot take allopurinol or do not reach target on a fully adjusted dose; in the United States it carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death and is restricted to those situations.
xanthine-oxidase-inhibitors.mechanism: Xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid at the end of purine breakdown. Blocking it drops blood urate below its saturation point, so no new crystals form and existing deposits slowly dissolve. Attacks can increase for the first months as crystals mobilise, so an NSAID or colchicine is given as cover, and the dose is raised until the urate target is reached. Allopurinol itself is cleared from the blood within hours, but the liver rapidly oxidises it to oxypurinol, an active metabolite that also blocks xanthine oxidase and persists for most of a day, which is why once-daily dosing works and why the drug accumulates when kidney function is poor. A second, smaller contribution comes from the incorporation of hypoxanthine and xanthine into nucleic acids, which feeds back to suppress new purine synthesis. Oxypurinol is also central to the class's most feared harm: in people carrying the HLA-B*58:01 allele, which is most common in those of Korean, Han Chinese or Thai descent, it is thought to bind the HLA molecule and alter its shape so that CD8 T cells attack the skin, producing Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis or the broader allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (fever, rash, eosinophilia and organ involvement), which carries a substantial mortality. Reduced kidney clearance lets oxypurinol accumulate, which is why the starting dose is cut in kidney disease and increased slowly. Febuxostat is a non-purine inhibitor of the same enzyme; a large cardiovascular outcome trial in people with gout and established cardiovascular disease found more cardiovascular deaths, most often sudden cardiac death, than with allopurinol, which led the US FDA to add a boxed warning, require a patient medication guide and limit its use to people with an inadequate response to a maximally adjusted allopurinol dose, intolerance to allopurinol, or in whom allopurinol is not advisable.

bisphosphonates.name: Bisphosphonates
bisphosphonates.summary: Medicines that slow bone loss by disabling the cells that dissolve bone, cutting hip and spine fractures in osteoporosis and treating Paget's disease and cancer in bone.
bisphosphonates.mechanism: Bisphosphonates bind bone mineral; when osteoclasts resorb that surface they absorb the drug, which disables their metabolism and triggers their death. Resorption falls while bone-building continues for a time, so density rises a few per cent and the bone's fine architecture is preserved. Weekly alendronate and risedronate, monthly ibandronate and yearly zoledronic acid infusions are the main forms.

macrolides.name: Macrolides
macrolides.summary: Antibiotics that stop bacteria making proteins by binding the bacterial ribosome, used for chest, ear, skin and sexually transmitted infections and as the main alternative in penicillin allergy. Azithromycin, clarithromycin and erythromycin differ mainly in how long they last and how much they interact with other medicines.
macrolides.mechanism: Macrolides bind the 23S ribosomal RNA in the exit tunnel of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and block the growing peptide chain, halting protein synthesis; the effect is bacteriostatic against most organisms. They concentrate inside cells, including the white cells that travel to infected tissue, so they work against intracellular pathogens such as Mycoplasma, Chlamydia and Legionella that penicillins cannot reach. Erythromycin and clarithromycin are strong inhibitors of the liver enzyme CYP3A4 and of P-glycoprotein and so raise the levels of statins, calcium channel blockers, warfarin, some anticoagulants and many other drugs; azithromycin barely inhibits CYP3A4 and interacts less. All macrolides can prolong the QT interval. Long-term low-dose azithromycin has anti-inflammatory effects used in COPD and bronchiectasis.

vaccines-influenza.name: Influenza vaccines
vaccines-influenza.summary: Seasonal vaccines against influenza A and B, reformulated every year: inactivated injected vaccines for most people and a live attenuated nasal spray for children. In the UK programme the nasal spray is the preferred vaccine for children of nursery and school age and for children with long-term conditions such as asthma needing a steroid inhaler or tablets, cystic fibrosis, serious heart disease, kidney or liver disease, diabetes or a weakened immune system; babies and toddlers below the spray's age range, and children for whom the spray is unsuitable, receive an injected vaccine instead. Vaccinating children protects not only them but the babies and older people around them. Protection takes about two weeks to develop and a new vaccine is needed every year because the circulating strains change. Side effects are mild and short-lived, serious reactions are rare, and every vaccinator is trained to recognise and treat an allergic reaction immediately.
vaccines-influenza.mechanism: Each formulation presents the immune system with haemagglutinin from the strains expected that season, either as inactivated virus fragments or, in the nasal spray, as weakened live viruses that replicate only in the cooler nose. Antibodies and memory cells form over about two weeks; the antibodies neutralise the virus at the airway surface and the memory cells speed the response if infection occurs. Because circulating strains drift, the strains are reselected annually and immunity from one season fades. The live attenuated viruses in the nasal spray are cold-adapted, so they multiply in the nose but not in the warmer lower airway, producing immunity in a similar way to natural infection but without the illness; they can also be shed for a short period, which is why children who have had the spray are advised to avoid close contact with very severely immunosuppressed people for about two weeks, and why staff who are themselves very severely immunosuppressed do not administer it. Because the spray relies on viral replication, anything that prevents it blunts the response: heavy nasal congestion from infection or allergy can impede delivery, and influenza antiviral drugs inactivate the vaccine viruses, so the spray is deferred until the antiviral course has been finished for a couple of days or an inactivated vaccine is given when protection is needed immediately. Aspirin and related salicylates are avoided in children after the live vaccine because of the association with Reye's syndrome. Most inactivated vaccines are grown in eggs, but the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation has concluded that egg allergy is no longer a contraindication to any influenza vaccine used in the UK and that there is no need to ask about it before vaccinating. The spray contains a highly processed porcine gelatine as a stabiliser; families who object on those grounds are offered an inactivated alternative.

contrast-agents.name: Contrast agents
contrast-agents.summary: Substances given to make blood vessels, organs, the gut or joints stand out on imaging: iodinated agents for X-ray and CT, gadolinium agents for MRI, microbubbles for ultrasound and barium for the gut. Modern intravascular iodinated agents are non-ionic and of low or iso-osmolality, which is why severe reactions are now uncommon; gadolinium agents are chelates whose structure (macrocyclic versus linear) governs how much gadolinium is left behind in the body. Because the kidneys clear both iodinated and gadolinium agents, kidney function and risk factors such as diabetes, heart disease, asthma and previous reactions are checked on a safety questionnaire before the injection, and the benefit of the information gained is weighed against a small risk for each person.
contrast-agents.mechanism: Each agent changes how the tissue it fills interacts with the imaging energy. Iodine and barium absorb X-rays, so filled vessels and cavities appear bright on X-ray and CT; gadolinium shortens the relaxation time of nearby water protons, brightening perfused tissue on MRI; microbubbles reflect ultrasound strongly and outline blood flow. Timing the scan to when the agent is in arteries, veins or tissue shows different structures. Iodinated agents are given into a vein, an artery, a joint or a body cavity and are eliminated by the kidneys, so a person with normal kidneys clears them quickly; a blood test may be used beforehand to confirm this. Gadolinium is itself toxic, so it is bound in a chelate: macrocyclic agents (gadoterate, gadobutrol, gadoteridol, gadopiclenol) hold it most tightly and leave the least residue, while linear agents release more and are associated with greater retention in bone, brain, skin, kidney, liver and spleen. The US regulator concluded that this retention has not been linked to harm in people with normal kidney function but required class warnings, patient medication guides and advice to avoid closely repeated studies where possible; the established serious hazard of gadolinium is nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in people whose kidneys cannot eliminate it. Immediate reactions to iodinated agents are mostly mild (nausea, vomiting, hives, itch, cough); moderate and severe reactions are much rarer, and the idea of an 'iodine allergy' is not supported by evidence and can lead to contrast being withheld unnecessarily. Kidney injury after contrast is a sudden fall in function within a day or two of exposure; large matched studies suggest it is far less frequent than once believed, and the diagnostic benefit of a well-chosen contrast study is judged to outweigh the risk for almost everyone.

radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.name: Diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals
radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.summary: Radioactive medicines given in tiny amounts so that a gamma camera or PET scanner can show where they accumulate: bone turnover, blood flow to the heart, thyroid activity, glucose use by tumours. Two technologies dominate. Technetium-99m, a pure gamma emitter with a short half-life, is the workhorse of gamma-camera and SPECT imaging of the brain, bones, lungs, kidneys, thyroid and heart and labels the great majority of tracers in routine use. Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a positron emitter, is the standard PET tracer: cancer cells take up more glucose than normal cells, so FDG accumulates in them, which makes PET-CT particularly useful for finding how far a confirmed cancer has spread and how it is responding to treatment, and for mapping the brain's glucose metabolism in suspected neurodegenerative disease. The injected tracer itself has no known side effects in most cases and allergic reactions are extremely rare; the main consideration is a small radiation dose.
radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.mechanism: A radioactive isotope is attached to a molecule the body handles in a known way: a phosphate analogue that binds forming bone, a glucose analogue trapped in metabolically active cells, iodine taken up by the thyroid, or a compound retained by well-perfused heart muscle. The radiation the isotope emits is detected from outside and mapped, so the image shows function rather than anatomy; combining it with CT adds the anatomy. The radiation dose is kept low by using short-lived isotopes and small amounts. Technetium-99m is useful because of its physics: a short half-life and a single gamma photon of an energy well suited to gamma cameras, so good images are obtained at low radiation exposure, and it has little or no therapeutic effect. Any technetium that comes free of its carrier molecule (pertechnetate) collects in the salivary glands, thyroid and stomach, which can complicate interpretation, so quality control of each preparation matters. FDG behaves like glucose: it is taken into cells by the same transporters and, once phosphorylated, is trapped, so the PET signal maps glucose use. Tissues with naturally low metabolic activity, such as the liver and prostate, give little contrast and limit FDG's usefulness there, whereas a fall in uptake in particular brain regions is the pattern seen in neurodegenerative disorders. Because FDG competes with the body's own glucose, blood glucose is checked before injection; a high glucose or insulin level reduces uptake into the target tissue and degrades the scan. After the injection the person rests quietly for an hour or more without reading or conversation, because muscle activity, including talking, diverts tracer into working muscles. The scanner detects where the tracer does and does not gather, and the CT acquired in the same session supplies the anatomical map on which those functional findings are placed; the whole PET-CT visit typically takes a few hours.

androgens.name: Androgens
androgens.summary: Steroid hormones that act on the androgen receptor. Testosterone in its various forms replaces the testes' output in hypogonadism and masculinises the body in gender-affirming therapy for trans men and non-binary people; the same molecules misused at high doses for muscle building are the anabolic steroids.
androgens.mechanism: Androgens enter cells and bind the androgen receptor, a nuclear receptor that changes gene expression. In prostate, skin and hair follicles 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, and in fat, bone and brain aromatase converts some to oestradiol. UK practice uses testosterone itself in different forms: gel or patch, injected oil-based esters, implants and capsules. Anti-androgens block the receptor (spironolactone and cyproterone acetate in feminising therapy, bicalutamide in prostate cancer); finasteride and other 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors cut dihydrotestosterone.
androgens.target: The androgen receptor in prostate, testes, muscle, bone, skin, hair follicles, bone marrow and brain, in some tissues after conversion to dihydrotestosterone by 5-alpha-reductase
classEffects: Virilisation: deeper voice, facial and body hair, clitoral enlargement and cessation of periods in people assigned female at birth, wanted in masculinising therapy and in part irreversible
Acne and oily skin, scalp hair loss in those predisposed, fluid retention, weight gain and mood change
Erythrocytosis (raised haemoglobin and haematocrit), more marked with injections
Prostate enlargement and a rise in PSA in men; suppression of sperm production and testicular shrinkage
cautions: Contraindicated in prostate cancer and male breast cancer, and in pregnancy and breastfeeding
Haematocrit is monitored: erythrocytosis thickens the blood and raises clot risk, and the dose or interval is reduced if it climbs
Used with care in heart failure, hypertension, sleep apnoea and kidney or liver disease because of fluid retention; older oral (17-alkylated) androgens damage the liver
Gel can transfer to partners and children through skin contact
Testosterone is not contraception in trans men and non-binary people, and anyone with a cervix still needs cervical screening
Anabolic steroid misuse for muscle building harms the heart, liver, fertility and mood, and in women causes irreversible virilisation

classWarnings.text: Androgens raise the red cell mass; haemoglobin and haematocrit are checked before treatment and at intervals, and the dose or dosing interval is reduced if erythrocytosis develops.
Testosterone is contraindicated in men with prostate cancer or breast cancer; prostate examination and PSA are part of assessment and follow-up in older men.

classInteractions.effect: Androgens enhance the anticoagulant effect; INR is monitored more closely.
Androgens can lower blood glucose, so requirements may fall.

oestrogens.name: Oestrogens
oestrogens.summary: Steroid hormones that act on the oestrogen receptor. Estradiol and related oestrogens replace the ovaries' output after the menopause, treat genitourinary symptoms locally and feminise the body in gender-affirming care.
oestrogens.mechanism: Oestrogens diffuse into cells and bind nuclear oestrogen receptors, which switch genes on or off. Estradiol, the ovaries' own hormone, is used for replacement; estriol is a weaker oestrogen in vaginal creams; conjugated oestrogens are an oral mixture; ethinylestradiol resists liver breakdown, which suits the combined pill but makes it more thrombogenic, so it is not used in HRT or feminising therapy. Oestrogen makes the endometrium proliferate, so anyone with a uterus takes a progestogen with systemic oestrogen. Oral routes raise clotting factors in the liver, unlike patches, gel and spray.
oestrogens.target: Oestrogen receptors (ERα and ERβ) in the uterus, breast, bone, blood vessels, brain and liver
classEffects: Breast tenderness, nausea, bloating, headache, leg cramps and fluid retention, especially in the first months
Irregular bleeding in the first months of combined HRT; endometrial thickening if oestrogen is taken unopposed with a uterus
Raised clotting factors and venous thromboembolism risk with oral routes, and a small rise in stroke risk with oral HRT
Relief of hot flushes, improved vaginal and urinary symptoms, preserved bone density and, in feminising therapy, breast growth and fat redistribution
cautions: Previous or current breast cancer or other oestrogen-dependent cancer, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, untreated endometrial hyperplasia, active or recent venous thromboembolism and active liver disease
Systemic oestrogen without a progestogen when the uterus is present raises the risk of endometrial cancer
A transdermal route is chosen where clot risk is raised: previous clots, obesity, smoking, migraine with aura, older age or immobility; oestrogen is usually paused around major surgery
Combined HRT carries a small, duration-dependent increase in breast cancer risk that falls after stopping; breast awareness and screening continue
Enzyme-inducing medicines reduce oestrogen levels, and oestrogens can increase levothyroxine requirements

classWarnings.text: Oestrogens raise the risk of venous thromboembolism, most with oral preparations and least with transdermal ones; they are avoided in active or recent thromboembolism and a transdermal route is preferred where risk factors are present.

Systemic oestrogen taken without a progestogen by anyone who has a uterus increases the risk of endometrial cancer; combined HRT carries a small increase in breast cancer risk related to duration of use.

classInteractions.with: Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin, St John's wort)
classInteractions.effect: Increase oestrogen metabolism and lower its effect.
Oestrogens raise thyroxine-binding globulin, so the levothyroxine dose may need to rise; TSH is checked.
